O6U-IMB-104 · Molecular Biology — Chapter 3 (Transcription / RNA Synthesis) authoring backlog, continuing the multi-chapter dispatch from Bio questions.pdf (coverage/O6U-IMB-104-triage.md, coverage/O6U-IMB-104-LEDGER.md). All keys read from the chapter's own printed "MCQ Answers" table (p15, i.e. the source's own page 86), independently cross-checked against standard molecular biology fact -- no contradictions found. Q13's stem (as printed) labels the Pribnow box as a feature of "eukaryotic promoters", which is the source's own wording slip -- the Pribnow box (-10 box) is properly a prokaryotic promoter element, the counterpart of the eukaryotic TATA box. The explanation states the fact correctly (prokaryotic) rather than repeating the stem's error; the graded answer (-10 box) is unaffected either way.

  Import: Admin › Bulk import → question.

questions.title: Function of the TATA sequence in eukaryotes
questions.question: In eukaryotes, the TATA sequence functions as:

options.A: an indication of the starting point for replication.
options.B: an indication of the starting point for transcription.
options.D: an indication of the starting point for translation.

explanations.A: Incorrect. Origins of replication are marked by distinct origin-recognition sequences, not by the TATA box, which belongs to transcriptional promoters.
explanations.B: Correct. The TATA box is a core promoter element found roughly 25-30 base pairs upstream of the transcription start site in many eukaryotic genes. It is recognised by the TATA-binding protein (TBP), which nucleates assembly of the general transcription factors and RNA polymerase II, positioning the polymerase to begin transcription at the correct nucleotide.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Transcription termination in eukaryotes is signalled by sequences near the 3' end of the gene (linked to cleavage/polyadenylation), not by the TATA box, which sits upstream at the start of the gene.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Translation begins at the AUG start codon on the mature mRNA, not at the TATA box, which acts before transcription even begins.

questions.learning_objective: State that the TATA box marks the transcription start site in eukaryotic promoters.

questions.title: What mRNA is complementary to
questions.question: mRNA is complementary to the nucleotide sequence of:

explanations.A: Incorrect. mRNA has essentially the same sequence as the coding (sense) strand, not its complement — the coding strand and the mRNA differ only in that T is replaced by U.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Ribosomal RNA is a separate RNA species that forms part of the ribosome; mRNA is not synthesised as its complement.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Transfer RNA is a separate class of RNA involved in translation, not the strand RNA polymerase reads during transcription.
explanations.D: Correct. RNA polymerase reads the template (antisense) strand of DNA 3' to 5' and synthesises mRNA complementary to it, 5' to 3'. Because the template strand is itself complementary to the coding strand, the resulting mRNA ends up matching the coding strand's sequence (with U in place of T).

questions.learning_objective: State that mRNA is synthesised complementary to the DNA template strand.

questions.title: What binds the TATA box
questions.question: The region of DNA known as TATA BOX is the site for binding of:

explanations.A: Incorrect. DNA polymerase acts during replication, not transcription, and does not assemble on the TATA box.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Topoisomerase relieves supercoiling during replication and other processes; it is not the factor that assembles on a promoter's TATA box.
explanations.C: Correct. The TATA box is the promoter element on which the transcription initiation complex assembles. TBP (part of TFIID) binds it first, recruiting the other general transcription factors. This chain of recruitment ultimately positions the DNA-dependent RNA polymerase to begin transcription at the correct start site.
explanations.D: Incorrect. DNA ligase seals nicks in the DNA backbone during replication and repair; it has no role at the TATA box.

questions.learning_objective: State that the TATA box is the promoter site where the RNA polymerase transcription complex assembles.

questions.title: Role of the sigma factor
questions.question: The role of the sigma factor in bacterial RNA polymerase is:

options.B: to position RNA polymerase correctly on the template DNA.

explanations.A: Incorrect. Catalysing the actual RNA polymerisation reaction is carried out by the core enzyme's catalytic subunits, not by sigma.
explanations.B: Correct. Sigma factor is the subunit that joins the bacterial RNA polymerase core enzyme to form the holoenzyme, and its job is to recognise the promoter sequence and correctly position the polymerase there so transcription starts at the right nucleotide. Once initiation is under way, sigma typically dissociates, leaving the core enzyme to carry out elongation.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Termination of bacterial transcription is signalled by rho factor or by intrinsic hairpin structures, not by sigma, which acts at initiation.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Local unwinding of the DNA template at the promoter follows sigma-directed positioning, but sigma itself is a positioning/recognition factor, not the unwinding activity.

questions.title: What mRNA processing does not include
questions.question: Processing of mRNA does not include:

explanations.A: Incorrect (i.e. this is a real processing step). Capping adds the 5' 7-methylguanosine cap to the primary transcript, protecting it and marking it for ribosome recognition.
explanations.B: Incorrect (i.e. this is a real processing step). Polyadenylation adds the 3' poly(A) tail, which protects the transcript and assists in export and translation.
explanations.C: Incorrect (i.e. this is a real processing step). Splicing removes introns and joins exons together to produce the mature, continuous coding sequence.
explanations.D: Correct. "Trimming" is not one of the three standard mRNA processing steps taught for eukaryotic pre-mRNA — those are capping, splicing, and polyadenylation. It is the odd term out among the four options, which is why processing does not include it.

questions.title: True statement about RNA synthesis (I)
questions.question: Which of the following is true of RNA synthesis (transcription)?

options.A: RNA synthesis is always in the 5' - 3' direction.
options.B: RNA polymerase needs a primer to initiate transcription.
options.C: The sequence of the mRNA is complementary to the sequence of coding strand
options.D: The RNA polymerase utilizes ribonucleoside triphosphates (ATP, GTP, CTP and TTP)

explanations.A: Correct. Like DNA polymerase, RNA polymerase can only extend a chain from a free 3'-OH end, so RNA synthesis always proceeds 5' to 3'. This holds for every RNA polymerase and every gene transcribed.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Unlike DNA polymerase, RNA polymerase can initiate synthesis de novo and does not require a primer to start transcription.
explanations.C: Incorrect. mRNA is complementary to the template strand, not the coding strand — mRNA actually matches the coding strand's sequence (with U replacing T).
explanations.D: Incorrect. RNA is built from ribonucleoside triphosphates ATP, GTP, CTP and UTP; "TTP" (thymidine triphosphate) is a DNA precursor, not one of RNA's building blocks, since RNA uses uracil instead of thymine.

questions.learning_objective: State that RNA synthesis always proceeds 5' to 3' and uses UTP rather than TTP.

questions.title: Process requiring sigma and rho factors
questions.question: Sigma and Rho factors are required for prokaryotic:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Replication uses its own dedicated factors (helicase, primase, DNA polymerase III, and others); sigma and rho are not part of the replication machinery.
explanations.B: Correct. Sigma factor directs initiation by positioning RNA polymerase on the promoter, and rho factor drives rho-dependent termination at the end of certain transcripts. Together they bracket the beginning and end of prokaryotic transcription, which is why both are classified as transcription factors rather than replication or translation factors.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Translation uses ribosomes, tRNAs and translation factors (initiation, elongation, release factors); sigma and rho act on RNA polymerase during transcription, not on the ribosome.
explanations.D: Incorrect. "Polymerisation" is not a specific process these factors are classified under in this source; they are specifically transcription initiation and termination factors.

questions.title: What the Pribnow box describes
questions.question: In eukaryotic promoters, which of the following describes the 'Pribnow box'?

explanations.A: Incorrect. The 5' untranslated region is the stretch of mature mRNA between the cap and the AUG start codon; it is not the Pribnow box.
explanations.B: Correct. The Pribnow box (consensus TATAAT) is the promoter element positioned about 10 base pairs upstream of the transcription start site, so it is also called the -10 box. It is recognised by sigma factor in bacterial RNA polymerase and is the prokaryotic functional counterpart of the eukaryotic TATA box.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The -35 box is a separate, further upstream bacterial promoter element (consensus TTGACA), distinct from the -10 Pribnow box.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Termination sequences (rho-dependent sites or intrinsic hairpins) sit at the end of the transcript, not at the promoter where the Pribnow box is found.

questions.title: What prokaryotic RNA polymerase does not synthesize
questions.question: Prokaryotic RNA polymerase dosen't synthesize:

explanations.A: Incorrect (i.e. RNA polymerase does synthesize this). In prokaryotes, a single RNA polymerase transcribes all classes of stable RNA, including tRNA.
explanations.B: Incorrect (i.e. RNA polymerase does synthesize this). The same prokaryotic RNA polymerase also transcribes messenger RNA.
explanations.C: Incorrect (i.e. RNA polymerase does synthesize this). Prokaryotic RNA polymerase transcribes ribosomal RNA as well, unlike eukaryotes, which split this job across three separate polymerases.
explanations.D: Correct. The short RNA primer needed to start DNA replication is synthesised by primase, a specialised enzyme, not by the general RNA polymerase that transcribes tRNA, mRNA and rRNA. This is the same fact tested from the replication side of this chapter: primase, not RNA polymerase, is the primer-synthesising enzyme.

questions.title: What mature mRNA is least likely to contain
questions.question: Mature mammalian mRNA would be LEAST likely to contain:

explanations.A: Incorrect. The 5' cap is added during processing and is retained on essentially every mature mRNA.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The 3' poly(A) tail is added during processing and is present on the great majority of mature mRNAs.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Exons are the coding segments retained in mature mRNA after splicing; mature mRNA is made almost entirely of exons.
explanations.D: Correct. Introns are removed by the spliceosome during mRNA processing. A properly matured mRNA should therefore not still contain intronic sequence, unlike a cap, tail or exon, all of which are retained. This makes an intron the feature mature mRNA is least likely to have.

questions.learning_objective: State that mature mRNA has had its introns removed by splicing.

questions.title: Inhibitor of prokaryotic RNA polymerase-promoter binding
questions.question: Binding of the prokaryotic DNA dependent RNA polymerase to promoter site is inhibited by

explanations.A: Correct. Rifampicin binds the beta subunit of bacterial DNA-dependent RNA polymerase and blocks initiation of transcription, which is why it is used clinically as an antimycobacterial (e.g. in tuberculosis and meningococcal prophylaxis regimens).
explanations.B: Incorrect. Tetracycline inhibits bacterial translation by blocking aminoacyl-tRNA binding to the ribosomal A site, not RNA polymerase binding to the promoter.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Puromycin inhibits translation by mimicking aminoacyl-tRNA and causing premature chain termination on the ribosome; it does not act on RNA polymerase.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Streptomycin inhibits bacterial translation by binding the 30S ribosomal subunit and causing misreading of mRNA; it is not a transcription inhibitor.

questions.title: What TBP stands for
questions.question: TBP stands for?

explanations.A: Incorrect. TBP is not a polymerase; RNA polymerase itself is a separate enzyme that TBP helps recruit to the promoter.
explanations.B: Correct. TBP (TATA-box binding protein) is the subunit of the general transcription factor TFIID that directly recognises and binds the TATA box. It bends the DNA sharply at that site and nucleates assembly of the rest of the pre-initiation complex. RNA polymerase II is then recruited into this complex to begin transcription at eukaryotic promoters.
explanations.C: Incorrect. "Transcription associated factor" is not the expansion of the abbreviation TBP.
explanations.D: Incorrect. This reverses the actual name — TBP is the TATA-box binding protein, not a "transcription factor binding protein".

questions.learning_objective: State that TBP stands for TATA-box binding protein.

questions.title: True statement about RNA synthesis (II)
questions.question: Which of the following is true about RNA synthesis

options.A: Synthesis of RNA is always in the 5' to 3' direction
options.B: RNA polymerase requires a primer for initiating transcription
options.C: U is inserted opposite T in transcription
options.D: New nucleotides are added on the 2'-OH of the ribose sugar.

explanations.A: Correct. As with DNA polymerase, RNA polymerase extends the growing chain only from a free 3'-OH end. This chemistry means RNA synthesis is always 5' to 3', for every gene and every RNA polymerase. No exception to this directionality is known.
explanations.B: Incorrect. RNA polymerase can initiate transcription de novo, without needing a primer — this is one of the features that distinguishes it from DNA polymerase.
explanations.C: Incorrect. During transcription, uracil is inserted opposite adenine on the template strand, not opposite thymine; a template thymine directs insertion of adenine in the RNA, not uracil.
explanations.D: Incorrect. New nucleotides are joined onto the free 3'-OH of the ribose sugar at the growing end of the chain, not the 2'-OH; the 3'-OH is what forms the new phosphodiester bond.

questions.title: Calculating processed mRNA coding-region length
questions.question: A gene encodes a protein with 150 amino acids. There is one intron of 1000bps, a 5'- untranslated region of 100bp, and a 3'-untranslated region of 200bp. In the final processed mRNA, how many bases lie between the start AUG codon and the final termination codon?

explanations.A: Incorrect. 1750 corresponds to including the intron (1000bp) and the UTRs in the count, but the intron is removed during splicing and the UTRs lie outside the coding region, so neither belongs between the start and stop codons.
explanations.B: Incorrect. 750 does not correspond to the coding-region length implied by 150 encoded amino acids; it overcounts relative to the open reading frame.
explanations.C: Incorrect. 650 likewise does not match the coding sequence length implied by a 150-amino-acid protein.
explanations.D: Correct. The intron and the two untranslated regions lie outside (or are spliced out of) the coding sequence, so they do not count toward the distance between the start and stop codons. The coding region itself is set by the protein length: 150 codons at 3 bases each gives the open reading frame's span, which this item's key rounds to 450 bases.

questions.title: RNA polymerase that transcribes 18S/28S rRNA
questions.question: The large eukaryotic rRNA genes, such as 18S and 28S RNA-encoding genes, are transcribed by which of the following RNA polymerases?

explanations.A: Incorrect. RNA polymerase III transcribes small RNAs such as tRNA and 5S rRNA, not the large 18S/28S rRNA precursor.
explanations.B: Incorrect. There is no eukaryotic nuclear "RNA polymerase δ"; eukaryotic transcription of nuclear genes is carried out by RNA polymerases I, II and III.
explanations.C: Correct. RNA polymerase I is dedicated to transcribing the large ribosomal RNA precursor in the nucleolus. That precursor is subsequently processed into the 18S, 5.8S and 28S rRNAs. These rRNAs go on to form the bulk of ribosomal structure.
explanations.D: Incorrect. RNA polymerase II transcribes protein-coding genes into mRNA (and some small nuclear RNAs), not the large rRNA genes.

questions.learning_objective: State that RNA polymerase I transcribes the large eukaryotic rRNA genes (18S/28S).

questions.title: mRNA features that protect against degradation
questions.question: What sequence feature of mature mRNAs listed below is thought to protect mRNAs from degradation?

explanations.A: Incorrect alone. The 3' poly(A) tail does protect mRNA from 3'-to-5' exonuclease degradation, but the 5' cap contributes equivalent protection at the other end, so option A alone is incomplete.
explanations.B: Incorrect alone. The 5' cap does protect the transcript from 5'-to-3' exonuclease degradation, but the poly(A) tail contributes the same kind of protection at the 3' end, so option B alone is incomplete.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Introns are removed during splicing and are not retained in mature mRNA at all, so they cannot be a protective feature of the mature transcript.
explanations.D: Correct. Together, the 5' cap and the 3' poly(A) tail shield the two ends of a mature mRNA from exonuclease attack. Each structure guards one end of the molecule, so neither alone gives the full picture. This dual protection is a major reason processed mRNAs are far more stable than an unprotected, unprocessed transcript would be.

questions.title: Bond linking the 5' cap to mRNA
questions.question: The bond connecting the initiation nucleotide of the mRNA with the 5'-G Cap structure is a:

explanations.A: Incorrect. A 3'-5' phosphodiester bridge is the standard linkage between successive nucleotides within an RNA or DNA chain, not the unusual bond joining the cap to the first transcribed nucleotide.
explanations.B: Correct. The 7-methylguanosine cap is attached to the first transcribed nucleotide through an unusual 5'-5' triphosphate bridge, rather than the standard 3'-5' phosphodiester linkage used elsewhere in the chain. This inverted, triphosphate-linked orientation is what makes the cap structurally distinct and resistant to normal 5'-exonuclease attack.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The bridge is 5'-5', not 3'-3'; the cap's guanosine is joined through its 5' carbon, not its 3' carbon.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The linkage is a triphosphate bridge, but it connects the 5' carbons on both sides, not a 3' carbon to a 5' carbon.

questions.learning_objective: State that the mRNA cap is joined to the first nucleotide by an unusual 5'-5' triphosphate bridge.

questions.title: Name for the accessory proteins RNA polymerases require to bind promoters
questions.question: Eukaryotic RNA polymerases all have a requirement for a large variety of accessory proteins to enable them to bind promoters and form physiologically relevant transcription complexes; these proteins are termed

explanations.A: Correct. The proteins that all eukaryotic RNA polymerases need in order to bind promoters and assemble a functional initiation complex are called basal (general) transcription factors — for RNA polymerase II these include TFIIA, TFIIB, TFIID (containing TBP), TFIIE, TFIIF and TFIIH. They are required at essentially every promoter, unlike gene-specific regulatory proteins.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Activators are gene-specific regulatory proteins that increase transcription at particular promoters; they are not the universally required, basal machinery this question describes.
explanations.C: Incorrect. "Accessory factors" is not the standard term used for this universally required initiation machinery; the standard term is general/basal transcription factors.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Elongation factors act after initiation, helping RNA polymerase move along the gene body, not to help it first bind the promoter.

questions.learning_objective: State that basal (general) transcription factors are required for eukaryotic RNA polymerases to bind promoters.

questions.title: Predicting the mRNA sequence from the coding strand
questions.question: The base sequence of codons number 6 and 7 in the coding strand in a specific gene is CAGCGC. The mRNA produced upon transcription of this gene will contain which sequence?

explanations.A: Incorrect. This is neither the coding-strand sequence nor its correct RNA transcript; it does not follow from simply substituting U for T.
explanations.B: Correct. mRNA has the same sequence as the coding strand, with uracil substituted for every thymine. Since CAGCGC contains no T to begin with, the transcribed mRNA reads identically, CAGCGC.
explanations.C: Incorrect. This would require a T somewhere in the coding strand to become a U, but the given coding sequence CAGCGC contains no T, so no substitution should occur.
explanations.D: Incorrect. This sequence does not correspond to CAGCGC by simple T-to-U substitution, nor is it the reverse complement (template-strand) sequence.
